q: Selecting items from the goods received note file and tracing them into the purchase ledger directly addresses which assertion?
o: Occurrence of the purchases recorded in the period
Existence of inventory held at the reporting date
Completeness of purchases and the related liabilities
Rights and obligations over the inventory on hand
why: Testing from source documents into the accounting records tests completeness because the risk is omission; tracing in the reverse direction from ledger to document would test occurrence.

q: The direction of testing best suited to detecting overstatement of trade receivables is:
o: Selecting from despatch records and tracing to the sales ledger
Selecting recorded balances and vouching to despatch notes
Reviewing the ageing report for balances over six months
Recomputing the interest charged on overdue balances
why: Overstatement is found by starting with recorded amounts and seeking support, which tests existence and occurrence; starting from source documents tests completeness and detects understatement.

q: Which set of assertions applies to account balances at the period end under SA 315?
o: Occurrence, completeness, accuracy, cut off and classification
Presentation, disclosure, aggregation and disaggregation
Occurrence and rights, completeness and understandability
Existence, rights and obligations, completeness, valuation
why: Balance assertions centre on existence, rights and obligations, completeness and accuracy valuation and allocation; occurrence and cut off belong to classes of transactions.

q: An auditor traces despatch notes dated in the first week after year end to the sales register to confirm they were excluded from current year sales. This primarily addresses:
o: Cut off for revenue and occurrence of the recorded sales
Valuation of the related trade receivables at year end
Rights and obligations over the goods despatched later
Classification of sales between reportable segments
why: Testing post year end despatches for inclusion in the current year targets cut off and would reveal revenue booked before control transferred, an occurrence failure.

q: The rights and obligations assertion for inventory is best tested by:
o: Attending the physical count and observing the procedures
Testing the standard cost roll and variance absorption
Examining supplier and consignment arrangements on site
Reviewing the ageing profile of slow moving stock lines
why: Consignment stock and goods on approval sit on the premises without being owned, so contractual review addresses rights; counting tests existence, costing tests valuation and ageing tests net realisable value.

q: Which of the following is a presentation assertion rather than one relating to transactions or balances?
o: Cut off of transactions around the reporting date
Existence of the recorded assets at that date
Accuracy of the amounts recorded in the ledger
Classification and understandability of disclosures
why: Presentation assertions cover occurrence and rights of disclosed matters, completeness of disclosure, classification and understandability, and accuracy and valuation of disclosures.

q: External confirmation of a bank balance provides the strongest evidence for which combination of assertions?
o: Completeness and valuation of all the cash balances
Cut off and classification of banking transactions
Existence and rights, with little on completeness
Accuracy and valuation to the exclusion of all else
why: A bank confirmation evidences the existence of the confirmed balance and the entity right to it, but not completeness, because undisclosed accounts would never be circularised.

q: For a construction contract measured on a percentage of completion basis, the assertion most at risk is:
o: Accuracy and valuation, given judgement over progress
Existence of the related contract receivable balances
Classification between current and non current items
Rights and obligations over the recognised contract asset
why: Revenue and contract asset amounts depend on estimated total costs and measured progress, so subjective valuation drives the risk while the other assertions are comparatively mechanical.

q: Reviewing payments made in the two months after year end to see whether the related liability was recorded at the reporting date primarily addresses:
o: Existence of the trade payables that were recorded
Classification of the related expenses in the ledger
Cut off of the inventory receipts at the year end
Completeness of liabilities, the main payables risk
why: The subsequent payments search finds obligations that existed at the reporting date but were never recorded; payables carry an understatement rather than an overstatement risk.

q: Which procedure best addresses the completeness assertion for provisions against legal claims?
o: Recomputing the provision on the management assumptions
Lawyer confirmations, minutes and legal expense review
Comparing the closing provision with the prior year
Confirming settled claims were paid after the year end
why: Completeness requires a search for matters management may not have disclosed, which lawyer confirmations, minutes and legal expense scrutiny provide; recomputation only tests what is already recorded.

q: The accuracy assertion for a class of transactions means that:
o: All transactions that should be recorded have been recorded
Recorded transactions occurred and pertain to the entity
Amounts and related data have been recorded appropriately
Transactions are recorded in the correct accounting period
why: Accuracy concerns whether amounts and related data were recorded appropriately; the other options define completeness, occurrence and cut off respectively.

q: An auditor selects items from the fixed asset register and locates them physically on the factory floor. This tests:
o: Existence of the assets recorded in the register
Completeness of the fixed asset register itself
Valuation of the assets carried in the register
Rights and obligations over assets held on lease
why: Moving from the register to the floor confirms recorded assets exist; the reverse direction, from assets on the floor to the register, would test completeness.

q: A company offsets trade receivables and trade payables for the same counterparty without a legally enforceable right of set off. Which assertion is violated?
o: Existence of the trade receivables so presented
Completeness of the trade payables recorded
Classification and presentation of the amounts
Cut off of the underlying transactions posted
why: Both balances exist and are complete in the underlying records; the defect is improper offsetting, a presentation and classification failure that distorts the amounts on the face of the balance sheet.

q: Recalculating the expected credit loss allowance using entity default history and forward looking adjustments primarily supports:
o: Existence of the trade receivable balances
Rights and obligations over the receivables
Completeness of the recorded receivables
Accuracy, valuation and allocation of receivables
why: The allowance affects the carrying amount, so the procedure tests valuation and allocation; existence, ownership and completeness of the gross balances need different procedures.

q: For revenue, the occurrence assertion is most at risk where:
o: Bill and hold or channel stuffing inflates year end sales
Sales run through a controlled platform with despatch matching
Sales returns are processed shortly after the reporting date
Discounts are applied inconsistently between the customers
why: Bill and hold and channel stuffing record revenue where control has not transferred, so the transactions did not properly occur; inconsistent discounts affect accuracy and later returns affect estimates.

q: Which mapping of a procedure to an assertion is INCORRECT?
o: Observing the inventory count maps to existence
Inspecting title deeds maps to rights and obligations
Testing sales either side of year end maps to cut off
Testing receivables ageing maps to completeness
why: Ageing analysis supports valuation through the assessment of recoverability rather than completeness; the other three mappings are correct.

q: To obtain evidence that all employee benefit liabilities have been recorded, the most effective procedure is to:
o: Vouch a sample of recorded accruals to payroll records
Confirm outstanding balances with individual employees
Reconcile headcount and payroll to statutory returns
Recompute the gratuity provision on the prior year base
why: Completeness needs an independent source capable of revealing omissions, which headcount, statutory filings and actuarial reports supply; vouching recorded items cannot detect what was never recorded.

q: Which statement about the relationship between assertions and audit procedures is most accurate?
o: Each audit procedure evidences exactly one assertion only
A procedure can evidence several assertions but not substitute
Analytical procedures address all assertions equally well
Tests of controls directly evidence the monetary accuracy of items
why: Inspecting a sales invoice can evidence occurrence and accuracy together, yet strong existence evidence never substitutes for missing completeness work; controls testing evidences the control, not the amount.
